title: The government will spend an extra $3.6 billion over a decade on new university places

Topic:Universities

Tue 30 Jun 2026 at 10:47am

The government has introduced legislation that will enforce hard caps on the number of students universities can enrol.  (ABC News: Billy Cooper)

The federal government is making big changes to Australian universities — pushing students away from the most popular campuses by limiting how many students they can take, while expanding access for regional and lower-socio economic students.

The proposed overhaul is designed to curb intense competition between universities, ease pressure on major campuses and ensure more students are trained closer to where they live.

It's also part of a much bigger goal: to double the number of university students by 2050.

"Under Bob Hawke and Paul Keating, the number of Australians finishing high school jumped from around 40 per cent to almost 80 per cent. That was nation changing. This is the next step," federal Education Minister Jason Clare said.

Education Minister Jason Clare says 80 per cent of the workforce will have a TAFE qualification or university degree by 2050. (ABC News: Ian Cutmore)

But critics warn the changes could have unintended consequences, limiting choice for students and discouraging some from enrolling altogether, all while further putting off what some describe as a "more urgent and necessary" reform.

Under the legislation, which was introduced into parliament late last week, universities will be given a hard cap on how many domestic students they can enrol under a new "managed growth" funding system.

Those numbers will be negotiated with a new bureaucracy called the Australian Tertiary Education Commission (ATEC), which will oversee funding and sector performance.

Mr Clare said it was designed to address aggressive "Hunger Games" style competition, where universities have been enrolling more students than they have Commonwealth funding for.

"There is no absolute ban on taking additional students, but the government will fine universities all their student contribution revenue earned from over-enrolled places," Monash University higher education expert Andrew Norton said.

Andrew Norton says the government will fine universities for over-enrolled places. (ABC News: Peter Drought)

The changes could reshape where students study, particularly in major cities where demand for the most prestigious universities — often the wealthy Group of Eight (Go8) — is highest.

With fewer spots available at top institutions, entry scores for popular courses are likely to rise further, increasing competition for school leavers, meaning some might not pursue university at all.

"While most university applicants will accept a second or lower preference course, that will not always happen. Some people will decide not to spend time and money on a course that is not what they really want," Professor Norton said.

The policy could push students away from the prestigious universities. (ABC News: Billy Cooper)

Vicki Thomson, the CEO of the Go8, is concerned the "interventionist approach" limits where students can study.

"If a kid from Tenant Creek wants to go to the University of Western Australia or the University of Adelaide, that should be their choice to do that," Ms Thomson said.

"They shouldn't be then directed to a different university."

The federal opposition agrees.

"It's a bizarre system that reminds me of the centrally planned models that used to exist in the socialist republics," shadow education minister Julian Leeser said.

But Vice Chancellor of the University of Canberra, Bill Shorten, said the reforms could increase diversity and reduce pressure on smaller institutions.

"Right now, many regional and suburban universities rely on high-volume, low-cost courses to subsidise smaller, high-cost disciplines," Mr Shorten said.

Bill Shorten says the changes will increase diversity and make sure people are trained closer to where they live. (ABC News: Alfred Beales)

"That model is not sustainable in the long term if big capital inner city universities simply use their market power to trample smaller universities."

Mr Shorten said a more coordinated system would help ensure critical workers are trained closer to where they're needed.

"If we are serious about ensuring regional and outer suburban Australia has the teachers, nurses, and essential workers it needs, we must train people in the communities they will serve," he said.

Alongside caps on enrolments, the government is proposing a major shift in how universities are funded.

In a move it likens to "Gonski for universities", it says it will spend $3.6 billion over a decade to educate more students from the bush and low socio-economic status (SES) suburbs.

"If you get the marks, or you've got the skills, you've got what it takes. You will get a place."

The needs-based funding measure is designed to educate more students from the bush, and low SES suburbs. (ABC News: Billy Cooper)

Universities will receive an extra base rate of $1,535 per low SES student, or $1,398 for students at regional campuses, with the amount topped up further if a student has a low ATAR or is Indigenous.

The funding is intended to help universities provide additional support and improve completion rates among students who are more likely to drop out.

However, Vice-Chancellor of Western Sydney University, George Williams, has questioned whether the funding will reach the students who need it most.

"One problem we have at the moment is the definition of equity students is just based upon the postcode of where you live," Professor Williams said.

George Williams is worried the money will not be "well-directed". (ABC News)

"That's a really blunt and problematic way of working out who needs support to go to university. It includes students from poor postcodes, who might be wealthy and students who live in rich postcodes, who might live in housing commission."

He said student welfare payments such as Youth Allowance also needed to rise, with his university supplying "tens of thousands" of meals each year, as almost half of its students faced food insecurity.

"It's really critical that this money is well directed, that the needs-based funding goes to the students in genuine need."

While the government is pursuing new funding and enrolment policies, it is yet to act on one of the most controversial parts of the current system — the Job Ready Graduates (JRG) scheme.

Introduced by the Morrison government, the policy lowered fees for some degrees but increased them for others, particularly in the arts and humanities.

Australian students are less satisfied with their university degrees than ever before, according to a long-running survey.

As a result, some students are paying more than $50,000 for degrees, while double degrees can cost up to $90,000.

Despite opposing the policy while in opposition, Labor has not announced a plan to overhaul it, meaning students enrolling in coming years will still face high HECS debts.

Professor Williams said the issue was a more urgent priority than some of the new reforms.

"That cost is so large, so significant, can take so long to pay off, and until it's fixed, we're actually going to be stopping people going to uni who should have the benefits of a life-changing education."

Industry analysis also highlighted cost-of-living pressures on students, with Universities Australia (UA) warning of a "double squeeze" from higher HECS debt and everyday expenses.

"[Students] are paying more to live and more to study," CEO Luke Sheehy said.

The government was approached for further comment.

The legislation has been introduced to parliament and is expected to be debated in coming months.

To pass the Senate and become law, the government will need likely need support from crossbench senators and the Greens, who have not indicated how they would vote.

The Greens have been pressuring the government to move on JRG.

However, universities are already preparing for the changes, with caps imposed by ATEC due to start in January next year.
